prompt: Should all high school students be required to take a creative arts class such as music, drama, or painting?
text:
Many people believe that schools should focus only on math, science, and reading. However, I think every high school student should be required to take at least one creative arts class. Art, music, drama, and design teach skills that students need in every career, not just in artistic fields.

First, creative arts classes build problem-solving ability. When a student sketches a design or writes a song, there is rarely one correct answer. They must experiment, make choices, and revise their work. This process trains the mind to approach unfamiliar problems with patience and imagination. Engineers, doctors, and business leaders all rely on these same habits every day.

Second, the arts improve communication and confidence. Drama asks students to speak clearly in front of others and to understand emotions different from their own. Music requires teamwork, because a band or choir only sounds good when everyone listens carefully. These experiences help students become more comfortable presenting ideas and working with people who think differently.

Some critics argue that a required arts class takes time away from core subjects. Yet a single course in a four-year schedule is a small investment, and many students who struggle in traditional classrooms discover strengths in the arts. For these students, a painting or theater class may be the reason they stay engaged in school at all.

Finally, the arts give people a way to understand culture and history. Studying a painting from the 1800s or a poem from another country connects students to the lives of people in other times and places. Requiring creative arts is not about producing professional artists. It is about developing well-rounded people who can think creatively, express themselves, and appreciate the world around them.

prompt: Should all high school students be required to take a creative arts class such as music, drama, or painting?
text:
The question of whether high school students should be required to complete a creative arts course has received considerable attention in recent educational debates. This essay argues that such a requirement is justified because creative arts education cultivates cognitive flexibility, interpersonal competence, and cultural understanding, all of which are essential to academic and professional success.

Firstly, the creative arts develop cognitive flexibility. Tasks such as composing music or designing a visual piece require learners to generate multiple solutions, evaluate their effectiveness, and revise accordingly. Research in cognitive development suggests that this iterative process strengthens divergent thinking, a capacity that transfers to disciplines well beyond the arts, including engineering, medicine, and business.

Secondly, arts education fosters interpersonal competence. Performance-based disciplines such as drama and ensemble music demand precise communication, emotional awareness, and collaborative discipline. Students who participate in these activities often demonstrate improved public speaking and greater comfort in group settings.

Opponents contend that a mandatory arts course reduces instructional time available for core subjects. This concern is legitimate, yet a single course within a standard curriculum represents a modest allocation, and the cumulative benefits may offset the opportunity cost. Moreover, for students who are disengaged from traditional academic content, the arts can provide a meaningful point of entry.

In conclusion, a required creative arts course offers broad educational value. It enhances cognitive, social, and cultural development, thereby preparing students for the demands of an increasingly complex society.

prompt: Should students be required to complete community service hours to graduate? Explain your position.

Should students be required to complete community service hours before they graduate? I believe the answer is yes, because service teaches responsibility, builds empathy, and strengthens the neighborhoods where students live. A graduation requirement ensures that every student gains these benefits, not only those who already have the time or motivation to volunteer.

Community service gives students a chance to see problems that they might never notice from inside their own routines. A student who spends a Saturday at a food bank learns how many families struggle to afford groceries. A student who helps tutor younger children learns that education is not equally available to everyone. These experiences often shift a young person's view of the world and of their own responsibilities.

Critics argue that required service turns a meaningful choice into a chore. They worry that students will count hours without caring about the work. This concern is worth taking seriously, and schools should design service programs that connect students to real projects and reflection. However, the answer is not to abandon the requirement. Many people who first volunteered because they had to later continued on their own because they found the work rewarding.

A service requirement also helps schools respond to real community needs. Libraries, animal shelters, parks, and senior centers depend on volunteers. When students contribute, they become part of the solution to local problems rather than observers of them.

In conclusion, graduation should include community service. The requirement asks students to give something back, and in return they gain skills, perspective, and a stronger sense of belonging to the place they call home.

prompt: What is one place you would recommend others visit, and why?
text:
If I could recommend one place for everyone to visit, it would be Kyoto, Japan. This historic city offers a rare combination of ancient temples, traditional gardens, and everyday life that has changed slowly over centuries. Visitors who take the time to explore it come away with a deeper appreciation for beauty, patience, and cultural continuity.

Kyoto was the capital of Japan for more than a thousand years, and its streets still reflect that long history. Walking through the Gion district in the early evening, visitors can see wooden machiya townhouses, lanterns glowing above narrow lanes, and occasionally a geisha hurrying to an appointment. The city has preserved much of its architecture, so the past feels present rather than locked inside a museum.

The temples are also remarkable. Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion, shines above a reflecting pond, while Fushimi Inari Shrine leads visitors through thousands of red torii gates winding up a forested mountain. Arriving early in the morning helps avoid crowds, and it allows a quiet moment to appreciate the calm that makes these places special.

Food is another reason to go. Small restaurants serve tofu dishes, seasonal vegetables, and noodles prepared with careful attention. Even a simple breakfast at a neighborhood shop can feel like a lesson in how much thought goes into daily life.

Kyoto is not perfect, and tourism can make some areas crowded. Still, travelers who slow down and respect local customs will find that the city rewards curiosity. It is a place that teaches people to look more closely at the world around them.

prompt: What is one place you would recommend others visit, and why?
text:
Among the many destinations available to contemporary travelers, Florence, Italy, merits particular recommendation. The city is distinguished by an extraordinary concentration of artistic, architectural, and historical achievement, and its significance extends well beyond tourism to the broader understanding of European cultural development.

Florence emerged as a major center of commerce and banking during the late medieval period, and its prosperity supported the flowering of the Renaissance. The Duomo, with its monumental dome designed by Filippo Brunelleschi, remains a landmark of engineering as well as art. Within a short walk, visitors may encounter the Uffizi Gallery, which houses major works by Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci, and Michelangelo.

The city's public spaces also reward careful observation. The Piazza della Signoria contains sculptures that reflect the civic identity of the Florentine republic, and the Ponte Vecchio, with its shops built along the river, illustrates the economic character of the medieval city. Such features allow visitors to interpret history through the physical environment.

Some critics argue that Florence is overcrowded, and this concern is legitimate, particularly during peak seasons. Nonetheless, travelers who plan visits thoughtfully, including early morning exploration and advance reservations, can experience the city with greater depth.

In conclusion, Florence offers an intellectually rich experience that combines artistic excellence with historical significance. It is a destination that rewards sustained attention and informed curiosity.

There's also this viewpoint called Miradouro da Senhora do Monte where you can see the whole city and the river. It was windy and I almost lost my hat, which I'm still a little annoyed about.

I guess what I'm trying to say is Lisbon feels lived in. It isn't a museum. People are hanging laundry out the windows and yelling at each other on balconies. I liked that a lot, even though I didn't really plan for it. Go. Bring comfortable shoes. And maybe skip the hat.

prompt: Should schools make extracurricular activities mandatory for all students?
text:
Should extracurricular activities be mandatory for all students? While such a requirement might seem to add pressure to already busy schedules, I believe schools should encourage every student to participate in at least one activity outside the classroom. Structured involvement in clubs, teams, and organizations builds skills and relationships that academic courses alone cannot provide.

Extracurricular activities teach students how to manage time, set goals, and work with others toward a shared purpose. A student on a debate team learns to research thoroughly and respond under pressure, while a member of a school band learns to practice consistently and perform in front of an audience. These experiences prepare young people for responsibilities they will face in college and in the workplace.

Activities also help students find a sense of belonging. Many young people feel isolated during their teenage years, and a club or team can provide a community where they feel valued. For students who are shy or struggle academically, these groups can become the most important part of their school experience.

Opponents argue that requiring participation removes freedom and places unnecessary strain on students who work jobs or care for family members. These concerns are valid, and any policy should provide flexible options. A requirement that allows students to choose among many activities, including volunteer work and independent projects, respects individual circumstances while still encouraging engagement.

In conclusion, requiring participation in at least one extracurricular activity would help students grow socially, emotionally, and intellectually. Schools should design this expectation thoughtfully so that it opens doors rather than closing them.

prompt: Should schools make extracurricular activities mandatory for all students?
text:
The question of whether extracurricular participation should be compulsory for secondary students invites careful consideration of both educational benefit and individual autonomy. This essay contends that while such participation yields considerable developmental advantages, a mandatory requirement would be counterproductive and should not be adopted.

Extracurricular involvement has been associated with improved academic engagement, leadership development, and social integration. Structured activities provide opportunities to practice collaboration, sustained commitment, and goal-directed behavior. Schools therefore have a legitimate interest in promoting such participation.

However, compulsion carries significant limitations. Motivation that originates externally is generally less durable than intrinsic motivation, and students who are required to participate in activities they find unappealing may derive limited benefit. Moreover, a uniform requirement fails to account for variation in students' circumstances, including employment obligations and familial caregiving responsibilities, which may render compliance burdensome or infeasible.

Alternative approaches may achieve similar outcomes without coercion. Schools may broaden the range of available options, reduce barriers to participation such as transportation and fees, and provide advisory support to help students identify suitable activities. Such measures are more likely to produce voluntary, sustained engagement.

In summary, although extracurricular participation is valuable, mandatory policies risk undermining the intrinsic motivation and individual circumstances on which meaningful involvement depends. Encouragement and improved accessibility represent a more defensible strategy.

prompt: If you could teach an elementary school class one lesson, what would it be and why?
text:
If I could teach one lesson to elementary school students, it would be how to handle mistakes with patience and curiosity. Many children believe that making an error means they are not smart or capable. Teaching them to see mistakes as useful information would help them become confident learners who are willing to try difficult things.

I would begin the lesson by asking the students to share a time they got something wrong. Some would describe spilling juice or forgetting a word during a spelling test. I would then explain that scientists, artists, and athletes all make mistakes regularly, and that these errors often lead to important discoveries. Learning to look at a mistake calmly is a skill that children can practice from an early age.

Next, I would give the class a simple activity. Students would build a tower from blocks, and then I would ask them to make it taller while the tower keeps falling. Each time it collapses, they would talk about what went wrong and try a different approach. This activity shows that persistence and reflection can produce better results than giving up.

To finish the lesson, I would ask each student to say one thing they learned from a mistake. The goal is to make the classroom feel safe for trying, asking questions, and admitting uncertainty.

Children who learn to treat errors as part of growth are more likely to remain curious throughout their education. This lesson may seem small, but it can shape how a child approaches challenges for the rest of their life.

prompt: If you could teach an elementary school class one lesson, what would it be and why?
text:
Should elementary education prioritize instruction in civic and environmental responsibility? If I were given the opportunity to design a single lesson for young learners, I would select the principle of stewardship, namely the recognition that individuals bear responsibility for the shared resources on which their communities depend. The lesson would be developmentally appropriate and grounded in direct experience.

The instructional sequence would begin with an observational activity in which students examine a classroom or schoolyard and identify items that could be reused, repaired, or disposed of responsibly. This exercise builds attentiveness and introduces the concept of resource cycles in a concrete manner. Students would then categorize materials by composition, which reinforces early classification skills.

The second phase would involve a narrative component. A brief account of a local waterway affected by pollution would prompt discussion of cause and consequence, allowing students to consider how individual decisions aggregate into collective outcomes. Teachers could then guide students to propose modest interventions, such as organizing a classroom recycling system.

The lesson would conclude with a collaborative project, in which students produce informational posters for distribution within their households. This extension integrates school learning with family engagement and reinforces the transfer of knowledge beyond the classroom.

Such an approach would cultivate environmental literacy and civic habits while remaining accessible to young children. The lasting value of the lesson lies in establishing a disposition toward responsible participation in communal life.

prompt: Should extracurricular activities be given grades on a student's report card?
text:
Should extracurricular activities receive grades on a student's report card? While it may seem fair to recognize effort in clubs and teams, I believe that assigning formal grades to these activities would undermine their purpose. Extracurricular involvement works best when students participate for personal growth, enjoyment, and genuine interest rather than for a mark on a transcript.

Grades create external pressure that can change how students approach an activity. A student who knows that a club leader will assign a score may focus on appearing productive rather than exploring new ideas. Creative and voluntary experiences, such as writing for the school newspaper or designing a robot, depend on freedom to experiment and sometimes fail. Assessment can narrow this freedom.

Grading also raises questions of fairness. Students have different levels of access to activities, and some depend on transportation, fees, or family support. A grade might reflect a student's circumstances rather than their commitment. Teachers and advisers would also face the difficult task of evaluating skills in very different settings, from debate to dance.

Nevertheless, recognition is valuable. Schools can acknowledge participation through certificates, written feedback, or letters of recommendation without placing a numerical grade on the report card. These forms of acknowledgment communicate appreciation while preserving the voluntary spirit of the activity.

In conclusion, extracurricular activities should be celebrated but not graded. Their greatest benefits come from the curiosity and commitment that students bring when no mark is at stake.

text:
The practice of assigning letter grades or numerical scores to extracurricular participation has been proposed as a means of encouraging commitment and accountability. This essay argues that such a practice would be inappropriate, as it compromises the intrinsic character of these activities, introduces problems of equity, and offers limited informational value.

Extracurricular programs are distinguished by their voluntary nature. Participants engage because of interest, personal goals, or a desire for social connection. The introduction of formal grading transforms these pursuits into evaluated obligations, which may diminish the autonomy and exploratory behavior that make them educationally valuable.

Equity considerations further weaken the case for grading. Access to extracurricular opportunities varies substantially according to financial resources, transportation, and family responsibilities. Grades derived from participation would therefore reflect, in part, students' socioeconomic circumstances rather than the quality of their engagement.

Moreover, the evaluation of activities as diverse as athletics, journalism, and performing arts presents considerable methodological difficulty. Standardized criteria would be difficult to establish, and subjective judgments could introduce inconsistency across programs.

Alternative forms of recognition, including certificates, narrative evaluations, and formal acknowledgment at school events, can document achievement while preserving the voluntary and developmental character of these activities. For these reasons, grading extracurricular participation is not recommended.

prompt: Is honesty always the best policy? Support your answer with examples.
text:
Is honesty always the best policy? Most people would answer yes, since honesty builds trust and respect. However, real life often presents situations where the truth is complicated, and the choice to be honest must be weighed against kindness, fairness, and consequences. In most cases, honesty remains the best policy, but it should be practiced with thoughtfulness rather than bluntness.

Consider a student who sees a classmate copy answers during an exam. Reporting the behavior may feel uncomfortable, but silence allows dishonesty to continue and harms students who study honestly. Here, honesty protects the fairness that every learner deserves. Similarly, a worker who notices a mistake in a company report should speak up, even when admitting the error is embarrassing, because hidden errors often grow larger over time.

Yet honesty does not require cruelty. When a friend asks whether a poorly written poem is good, a truthful response can still be gentle and constructive. Pointing out what works, suggesting specific improvements, and acknowledging the effort invested allow the truth to help rather than hurt. In this way, honesty and compassion can work together.

There are rare cases where withholding information may seem justified, such as when revealing a detail would endanger someone. Even then, the principle behind honesty, which is respect for others and for reality, remains important.

In conclusion, honesty is usually the best policy because it builds trust and allows people to make informed choices. When delivered with care, it strengthens relationships and communities.

prompt: Is honesty always the best policy? Support your answer with examples.
text:
The proposition that honesty constitutes an invariably optimal policy has long featured in moral philosophy and in ordinary social expectation. This essay argues that honesty is generally the most defensible course of conduct, since it sustains interpersonal trust, supports informed decision-making, and preserves institutional integrity, although its application must be tempered by considerations of compassion and proportionality.

The instrumental value of honesty is well established. Individuals and institutions that consistently communicate truthfully are more readily relied upon, and the discovery of deception tends to produce disproportionate and enduring damage to credibility. Within professional and academic settings, candor regarding error enables correction, whereas concealment frequently compounds the original harm.

Nonetheless, absolute adherence to literal disclosure may conflict with other moral goods. The obligation to be truthful does not necessarily entail an obligation to volunteer every relevant fact in every context. A communicator may legitimately select emphasis, timing, and framing, provided that such choices do not create false impressions. The distinction between withholding and deceiving is therefore central to a mature conception of honesty.

Certain circumstances, such as the protection of persons from imminent harm, may present genuine conflicts in which strict truthfulness is outweighed by other obligations. Such cases, however, remain exceptional rather than representative.

Accordingly, honesty should be regarded as a strong presumptive principle rather than an inviolable rule, and its practice should be guided by respect for both truth and the wellbeing of others.
